units:
Sustainable Development,
Equity & the Triple Bottom Line
The three ideas underneath every sustainability framework you will ever use
01

Every sustainability report, every ESG score, every 
climate lawsuit
relies on three ideas most people can't actually define.
By the end of today, you will be able to define all three precisely — and use them to judge whether a real decision is 
actually sustainable.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 02

T O D A Y ' S J O U R N E Y
Three Ideas, Built One on Top of the Other
01
Sustainable Development
The umbrella concept: meeting present needs 
without compromising the future.
02
Intergenerational Equity
The ethical engine inside that concept: fairness to 
generations not yet born.
03
The Triple Bottom Line
The measurement tool that turns the concept 
into something you can actually score.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 04

S E C T I O N 1 O F 3
Sustainable Development
The umbrella concept that gave the entire sustainability movement its shared vocabulary.
05

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E D E F I N I T I V E S O U R C E
The Brundtland Definition
The single most quoted sentence in the history of the sustainability movement.
"Development that meets the needs of the present
without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own 
needs."
The Source
"Our Common Future" (1987), also called the 
Brundtland Report — published by the UN World 
Commission on Environment and Development 
(WCED).
The Chair
Chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland, former Prime 
Minister of Norway — the commission was convened 
by the UN in 1983.
The Process
Nearly 900 days of research, public hearings, and 
consultation across 21 commissioner countries before 
publication in April 1987.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 06

S E C T I O N 1 · R E A D I N G I T C A R E F U L L Y
The Two Ideas Hidden Inside the Definition
The Brundtland Report itself immediately unpacked its own famous sentence into two essential concepts — both are usually forgotten.
The Concept of "Needs" In particular, the essential needs of the world's poor, to which overriding priority should be given. Sustainable 
development is not neutral between rich and poor — it explicitly prioritizes basic human needs first.
The Idea of "Limitations" Limitations imposed by the state of technology and social organization on the environment's ability to meet 
present and future needs. Sustainability is not a fixed ceiling — better technology and institutions can raise it.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 07

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E S T R U C T U R E
The Three Pillars of Sustainable Development
Nearly every sustainability framework since 1987 — including the Triple Bottom Line we cover later today — traces back to this three-way balance.
Environmental
Protecting ecosystems, biodiversity, and natural resources 
so they remain available and functional over time.
Social
Ensuring equity, health, education, and quality of life 
across all people — not just economic output.
Economic
Generating prosperity and livelihoods in a way that can 
continue indefinitely, not just in the short term.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 08

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E T O O L K I T
Core Principles of Sustainable Development
Beyond the definition, a small set of legal and policy principles operationalize sustainable development in practice.
The Precautionary Principle Where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should 
not be used as a reason to postpone preventive measures.
The Polluter Pays Principle The party responsible for producing pollution should bear the cost of managing it, rather than passing that cost 
on to society or the environment.
Intergenerational Equity Fairness between present and future generations — significant enough to be Section 2 of today's lecture in its 
own right.
Public Participation Environmental decisions should involve the people affected by them, with access to information and justice.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 09

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E I N D I A N C O N T E X T
Sustainable Development in Indian Law
Indian courts adopted these principles into binding law years before most other jurisdictions.
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India 
(1996)
The Supreme Court of India formally held that the Precautionary Principle and the Polluter Pays Principle are 
part of Indian environmental law.
Article 21 of the Constitution The Supreme Court has repeatedly interpreted the fundamental right to life to include the right to a clean and 
healthy environment.
The Public Trust Doctrine Indian courts (e.g., M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath, 1997) have held that certain natural resources are held by the 
state in trust for public use, including for future generations.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 10

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
According to the Brundtland Report itself, sustainable development 
gives "overriding priority" to which group's needs?
A Shareholders of large multinational corporations
B The essential needs of the world's poor
C Future generations exclusively, over the present generation
D National governments' economic growth targets
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. The essential needs of the world's poor
The Brundtland Report is explicit that the concept of 
"needs" centers "in particular the essential needs of 
the world's poor, to which overriding priority should 
be given" — sustainable development was never 
meant to be neutral between rich and poor.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 11

S E C T I O N 2 O F 3
Intergenerational Equity
The ethical engine hidden inside "sustainable development" — fairness to people who cannot yet speak for themselves.
12

S E C T I O N 2 · D E F I N I T I O N
What Is Intergenerational Equity?
A principle of fairness that extends across time, not just across a single population.
The Core Idea Each generation holds the Earth in trust for those that follow — present generations should not use up or 
degrade resources in ways that leave future generations worse off.
Why "Equity," Not Just "Sustainability" It reframes sustainability as a justice question: future people cannot vote, lobby, or buy carbon offsets today —
someone has to represent their interests now, on their behalf.
Where It Comes From Formalized as an international legal theory by Professor Edith Brown Weiss in her 1989 book, "In Fairness to 
Future Generations."
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 13

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E G O V E R N I N G F R A M E W O R K
Edith Brown Weiss's Three Principles
A precise, widely cited framework for what one generation owes the next.
Conservation of Options
Each generation should conserve the diversity of the 
natural and cultural resource base, so it does not unduly 
restrict the options available to future generations.
Conservation of Quality
Each generation should maintain the quality of the planet 
so that it is passed on in no worse condition than it was 
received.
Conservation of Access
Each generation should provide its members equitable 
rights of access to the legacy of past generations, and 
conserve this access for future generations.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 14

S E C T I O N 2 · A K E Y D I S T I N C T I O N
Intergenerational vs. Intragenerational Equity
Intragenerational Equity Intergenerational Equity
Fairness among people alive today — rich nations vs. poor, one community vs. 
another.
Fairness between generations across time — the present vs. those not yet 
born.
Example: should India and the US bear equal responsibility for emissions cuts 
today?
Example: should today's generation deplete oil reserves that future 
generations may need more?
Addressed by mechanisms like climate finance and "loss and damage" funds. Addressed by mechanisms like resource conservation, long-term planning, and 
discount-rate policy.
Both are required for sustainable development — one without the other is 
incomplete.
Both are required for sustainable development — one without the other is 
incomplete.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 15

S E C T I O N 2 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Why the Discount Rate Is an Ethical Choice
G I V E N
A policy prevents $1,000,000 of climate damage occurring in the year 2100 
(100 years away)
Stern Review (2006) used a low discount rate of approximately 1.4% per year
A higher, more traditional market-based discount rate: approximately 5% per 
year
F O R M U L A
Present Value = Future Value ÷ (1 + r)^t
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 At Stern's ~1.4% rate: $1,000,000 ÷ (1.014)^100 ≈ $249,000 in today's money
2 At a ~5% rate: $1,000,000 ÷ (1.05)^100 ≈ $7,600 in today's money
3 The identical future benefit is worth roughly 33× more under the low discount rate than the high one.
33× Difference Same future benefit, same year, same policy — but the choice of discount rate alone changes whether climate action looks 
"worth it" today by more than an order of magnitude.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 16

S E C T I O N 2 · E Q U I T Y I N P R A C T I C E
Intergenerational Equity in the Courts
What began as ethical theory is now active, binding litigation strategy worldwide.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (multiple cases) Indian courts have repeatedly invoked intergenerational equity alongside the public trust doctrine to justify 
environmental protection orders.
Urgenda Foundation v. State of the Netherlands 
(2019)
The Dutch Supreme Court ordered the government to cut emissions faster, citing its duty of care to both current 
and future citizens.
Youth-Led Climate Litigation Worldwide Cases brought by young people in multiple countries have argued that inadequate climate policy violates the 
constitutional rights of generations who will live with its consequences.

◆ INTERACTIVE T H I N K & S H A R E
"Youth climate litigation asks courts to protect 
people who are not yet born, or too young to vote. 
Should judges have that power — or should it stay 
with elected governments?"
There is no clean answer here. Notice the tension between democracy and long time horizons.

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
Which of Edith Brown Weiss's three principles is most directly 
violated by permanently destroying a unique ecosystem with no 
equivalent elsewhere?
A Conservation of Options
B Conservation of Quality
C Conservation of Access
D None of the three — biodiversity is outside this framework
A N S W E R & W H Y
A. Conservation of Options
Conservation of Options requires preserving the 
diversity of the natural resource base so future 
generations retain choices. Permanently destroying a 
unique, irreplaceable ecosystem directly forecloses 
options no future generation can ever recover.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 19

S E C T I O N 3 O F 3
The Triple Bottom Line
The measurement tool that turns "sustainable development" from a philosophy into a scorecard.
20

S E C T I O N 3 · O R I G I N S
What Is the Triple Bottom Line?
A simple, radical idea: a company's success should never be measured on profit alone.
People · Planet · Profit
The Coinage
John Elkington, founder of the consultancy 
SustainAbility, coined the term "triple bottom line" in 
1994.
The Book
Popularized in his 1997 book, "Cannibals with Forks: 
The Triple Bottom Line of 21st Century Business."
The Argument
Companies should report three separate bottom lines 
— economic, social, environmental — not just the 
financial one.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 21

S E C T I O N 3 · P I L L A R O N E
The Economic Bottom Line ("Profit")
Not just whether a company makes money — but whether it does so in a way that can continue indefinitely.
Traditional Financial Performance Revenue, profit margins, return on investment — the metrics every business already tracks.
Long-Term Economic Viability Can the business model survive resource price shocks, regulatory change, and reputational risk over decades, 
not just this quarter?
Value Created for the Wider Economy Wages paid, taxes contributed, suppliers supported — economic value the company generates beyond its own 
balance sheet.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 22

S E C T I O N 3 · P I L L A R T W O
The Social Bottom Line ("People")
How an organization treats the humans inside it, and the communities around it.
Fair Labour Practices Living wages, safe working conditions, freedom of association — and, across supply chains, freedom from forced 
or child labour.
Community Impact Effects on local health, housing, and livelihoods — both positive (local employment) and negative (pollution, 
displacement).
Diversity, Equity & Human Rights Fair treatment and opportunity regardless of gender, caste, ethnicity, or background, within the organization and 
its value chain.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 23

S E C T I O N 3 · P I L L A R T H R E E
The Environmental Bottom Line ("Planet")
The ecological footprint of an organization — everything covered in the rest of this course, in miniature.
Resource Use & Emissions Energy and water consumption, waste generated, and greenhouse gas emissions across Scope 1, 2, and 3.
Pollution & Ecosystem Impact Effects on air and water quality, biodiversity, and land use — both direct operations and the full supply chain.
Circularity & Resource Efficiency How much of what the organization uses is renewable, recycled, or designed to be reused, rather than extracted 
and discarded.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 24

S E C T I O N 3 · M E A S U R E M E N T
How the Triple Bottom Line Gets Measured
The idea only matters if it can actually be scored — these are the leading frameworks that do it.
GRI Standards
The Global Reporting Initiative — the 
most widely used framework worldwide 
for sustainability disclosure across all 
three pillars.
ESG Scores
Environmental, Social, and Governance 
ratings used by investors to price climate 
and social risk into company valuations.
B Corp Certification
A rigorous third-party certification 
verifying a company meets high 
standards of social and environmental 
performance, alongside profit.
India's BRSR
SEBI's Business Responsibility and 
Sustainability Reporting mandate —
India's own binding version of triple￾bottom-line disclosure.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 25

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
When a Company Restructured Around All Three Lines
Patagonia — "Earth Is Now Our Only Shareholder" (2022)
Founder Yvon Chouinard transferred 100% of Patagonia's voting stock to a specially designed trust, and all non-voting stock to a nonprofit — directing all profits 
not reinvested in the business toward fighting the climate crisis.
Economic ("Profit")
Patagonia remains a for-profit business, generating revenue to fund its own operations and 
growth — profit was never eliminated, only redirected.
Social ("People")
Long-standing fair labor and supply-chain standards, plus a governance structure explicitly 
designed to resist pressure to prioritize shareholder returns.
Environmental ("Planet")
An estimated ~$100 million/year in profit now flows to environmental causes and climate 
action instead of private shareholders.
The Lesson
A real example of ownership structure itself — not just a sustainability report — being 
redesigned around all three bottom lines simultaneously.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 26

S E C T I O N 3 · A C R I T I C A L L O O K
Even Its Inventor Has Doubts
In 2018, John Elkington published a Harvard Business Review article publicly "recalling" his own 25-year-old concept.
"The Triple Bottom Line has failed to bury the single bottom line paradigm... It was never supposed to be just an accounting system."
The Original Ambition
Elkington intended TBL to drive systemic transformation of capitalism itself — not just a 
reporting checklist.
What Actually Happened
Many companies reduced it to an "accounting tool" — adding social and environmental 
metrics to reports without changing core business models.
The Quantification Problem
Environmental and social impact are genuinely hard to express in the same monetary units 
as profit, inviting selective or superficial reporting.
The Greenwashing Risk
A polished sustainability report can create an appearance of responsibility that isn't backed 
by real change — the exact critique this course applies to weak carbon credits.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 27

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
In his 2018 Harvard Business Review article, what did John 
Elkington argue had happened to the Triple Bottom Line?
A It had been banned by most stock exchanges
B It had been reduced to an accounting tool instead of driving systemic change
C It had been fully achieved by all Fortune 500 companies
D It had been replaced entirely by the SDGs
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. It had been reduced to an accounting 
tool instead of driving systemic change
Elkington argued that TBL was intended as a "genetic 
code" to transform capitalism itself, but in practice 
was reduced by many companies to a reporting and 
accounting exercise — prompting him to publicly 
"recall" the concept for a rethink.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 29

B R I N G I N G I T T O G E T H E R
How the Three Ideas Actually Connect
Each concept plays a distinct, necessary role — none of the three is sufficient on its own.
Sustainable Development The umbrella goal Sets the overall destination: meeting present needs without compromising the future.
Intergenerational Equity The ethical justification Explains why the future matters morally, and gives it a voice in present-day decisions.
The Triple Bottom Line The measurement tool Turns the goal into something scoreable — three concrete lines a real organization can 
report against.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 30

◆ INTERACTIVE A P P L Y A L L T H R E E
"A mining company proposes a new project: 
strong local jobs and tax revenue, but it will 
deplete a resource future generations cannot 
replace. Using all three frameworks from today, 
how would you evaluate it?"
Consider: Brundtland's "needs," Weiss's conservation principles, and all three TBL pillars.

L E C T U R E R E C A P
Three Ideas, Recapped
1
The Brundtland Definition
Development meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future 
generations to meet their own.
2
Two Hidden Concepts
"Needs" (prioritizing the world's poor) and "limitations" (imposed by technology and 
social organization).
3
Three Pillars of SD
Environmental, Social, and Economic — the same three dimensions that reappear in the 
TBL.
4
SD in Indian Law
The Precautionary Principle and Polluter Pays Principle are binding law since Vellore 
Citizens (1996).
5
Intergenerational Equity
Fairness across time, not just across today's population — formalized by Edith Brown 
Weiss (1989).
6
Weiss's Three Principles
Conservation of Options, Quality, and Access — what one generation owes the next.
7
The Discount Rate Debate
A single technical choice can change the value of future harm by 30× or more — a 
hidden ethical decision.
8
The Triple Bottom Line
People, Planet, Profit — coined by Elkington (1994), popularized in "Cannibals with 
Forks" (1997).
9
The Elkington "Recall"
Even TBL's inventor warned it had become an accounting checklist instead of driving 
real transformation.
10 The Synthesis
Sustainable development is the goal, intergenerational equity is the ethics, and the 
Triple Bottom Line is the scorecard.
SUST AI N AB LE DE V E LOP ME N T · I N T E R GE NER ATI ONAL E Q UI T Y · T R I P LE B OT T OM LI N E 32

Principles of
Sustainability
Ecological Integrity · Resource Efficiency · Social Equity · Economic Viability
01

"Sustainable" is not one property.
It is four different tests a decision has to pass, all at 
once.
Today gives you the actual engineering and scientific vocabulary behind each test — the tools you'll use to judge 
whether something is genuinely sustainable, or just sounds like it.
PRINCIPLES OF SUSTAINABILITY 02

T O D A Y ' S J O U R N E Y
Four Principles, One Sustainability Test
These four principles sharpen the three Triple Bottom Line pillars from our last lecture into precise, usable engineering and policy criteria.
01
Ecological Integrity
Are ecosystems kept functioning, 
resilient, and intact?
02
Resource Efficiency
Is output achieved with less material, 
energy, and waste?
03
Social Equity
Are benefits and burdens shared fairly 
across all people?
04
Economic Viability
Can this actually continue, at its true, full 
cost?
PRINCIPLES OF SUSTAINABILITY 04

S E C T I O N 1 O F 4
Ecological Integrity
Whether the natural systems we depend on can keep functioning — not just whether individual species survive.
05

S E C T I O N 1 · D E F I N I T I O N
What Is Ecological Integrity?
More than "protecting nature" — a precise, measurable property of an ecosystem.
The Working Definition The maintenance of an ecosystem's composition (what species are present), structure (how they're organized), 
and function (nutrient cycling, energy flow) across time.
Why "Integrity," Not Just "Health" Integrity specifically includes resilience — an ecosystem's ability to absorb disturbance and recover, not just its 
condition at a single snapshot in time.
The Practical Test A system has ecological integrity if it can keep delivering its ecosystem services — clean water, fertile soil, 
climate regulation — under realistic future stress.
PRINCIPLES OF SUSTAINABILITY 06

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E S C I E N T I F I C F R A M E W O R K
The Planetary Boundaries Framework
Nine processes that regulate the stability of the entire Earth system — proposed by Johan Rockström and colleagues at the Stockholm Resilience Centre.
Climate Change Biosphere Integrity Land-System Change
Freshwater Change Biogeochemical Flows (N & P) Ocean Acidification
Atmospheric Aerosol Loading Stratospheric Ozone Depletion Novel Entities (Chemical Pollution)
● Transgressed (6 of 9) ● Within safe limits (3 of 9)
As of the 2023 Richardson et al. assessment (Science Advances), six of nine boundaries are transgressed — later tracking suggests a seventh (ocean acidification) may also now be crossed.
Source: Rockström et al. 2009; Steffen et al. 2015; Richardson et al. 2023, Science Advances.
PRINCIPLES OF SUSTAINABILITY 07

S E C T I O N 1 · W H Y I T M A T T E R S
Ecosystem Services We Depend On
Ecological integrity is not an abstract environmental concern — it is the infrastructure the entire economy runs on, for free.
Pollination
Roughly three-quarters of global food 
crop types depend at least partly on 
animal pollinators — a free service with 
no engineered substitute at scale.
Water Filtration
Wetlands and forested watersheds 
naturally filter pollutants and regulate 
water flow, avoiding costly built 
infrastructure.
Carbon Sequestration
Forests, soils, and oceans absorb a 
substantial share of human CO₂ 
emissions every year, at zero cost — until 
they're degraded.
Soil Fertility
Healthy soil ecosystems cycle nutrients 
that make agriculture possible at all — a 
service that took millennia to build and 
can be lost in years.
PRINCIPLES OF SUSTAINABILITY 08

S E C T I O N 1 · M A K I N G I T M E A S U R A B L E
How Ecological Integrity Gets Measured
Turning "is nature healthy?" into a number.
Species Richness & Abundance How many species are present, and in what numbers — a direct signal of ecosystem diversity and stability.
Habitat Connectivity Whether habitats are fragmented into isolated patches, or connected enough for species to migrate, breed, and 
adapt.
Resilience & Recovery Time How quickly a system returns to its prior state after a disturbance like fire, drought, or flood — the core of 
"integrity" itself.
PRINCIPLES OF SUSTAINABILITY 09

◆ INTERACTIVE T H I N K & S H A R E
"Of the six already-transgressed planetary 
boundaries, which do you think gets the least 
public attention relative to how serious it is —
and why?"
Climate change dominates headlines. What about the other five?
⏱ 3 MIN
PRINCIPLES OF SUSTAINABILITY 10

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
According to the 2023 Richardson et al. assessment, how many of the 
nine planetary boundaries have been transgressed?
A Three of nine
B Four of nine
C Six of nine
D All nine
A N S W E R & W H Y
C. Six of nine
The landmark 2023 study (Richardson et al., Science 
Advances) was the first to quantify all nine boundaries, 
finding six already transgressed: climate change, 
biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater 
change, biogeochemical flows, and novel entities.
PRINCIPLES OF SUSTAINABILITY 11

S E C T I O N 2 O F 4
Resource Efficiency
Achieving the same, or better, outcomes while extracting, consuming, and wasting less.
12

S E C T I O N 2 · D E F I N I T I O N
What Is Resource Efficiency?
Getting more human wellbeing and economic output out of every unit of material and energy consumed.
The Working Definition Maximizing the value delivered — goods, services, wellbeing — per unit of natural resource extracted, used, and 
discarded.
The Central Goal: Decoupling Breaking the historical link between economic growth and resource use or environmental harm, so the economy 
can grow while its footprint shrinks.
Relative vs. Absolute Decoupling Relative decoupling: resource use grows slower than the economy. Absolute decoupling: resource use falls even 
as the economy grows — the much harder, and more necessary, goal.
PRINCIPLES OF SUSTAINABILITY 13

S E C T I O N 2 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
The IPAT Equation: Reasoning About Impact
G I V E N
Population (P) grows by 10% over a decade
Affluence (A) — GDP per capita — grows by 20% over the same decade
Technology (T) — environmental impact per unit of GDP — improves (falls) by 
25%
F O R M U L A
Impact = Population × Affluence × Technology
(I = P × A × T)
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Express each factor as a multiplier: P = 1.10, A = 1.20, T = 0.75 (a 25% cut in impact intensity)
2 Multiply: I = 1.10 × 1.20 × 0.75 = 0.99
3 Net result: total environmental impact stays roughly flat — even slightly down — despite real growth in both population and wealth.
I ≈ 0.99×
Technology improvement alone offset a decade of population and income growth — this is exactly what "decoupling" looks like in 
the equation that first formalized the idea (Ehrlich & Holdren, 1970s).
PRINCIPLES OF SUSTAINABILITY 14

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E U N D E R L Y I N G M O D E L
Linear vs. Circular Economy
Linear Economy ("Take-Make￾Dispose") Circular Economy
Resources are extracted, used once, and discarded as waste at end of life. Products and materials are designed to be reused, repaired, remanufactured, 
or recycled.
Value is created once, then lost — the default model of most 20th-century 
industry.
Value is retained in the system for as long as possible — waste is designed out 
from the start.
"Waste" is treated as an unavoidable, external cost. One process's waste becomes another process's input — "industrial 
symbiosis."
Defined by contrast in the Ellen MacArthur Foundation's widely cited circular 
economy framework.
Defined by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation as: design out waste, keep 
materials in use, regenerate natural systems.
PRINCIPLES OF SUSTAINABILITY 15

S E C T I O N 2 · S E T T I N G T A R G E T S
Factor 4 and Factor 10: How Much Efficiency Is Enough?
Two influential targets for how far resource efficiency needs to go.
Factor 4 Proposed by von Weizsäcker, Lovins & Lovins (1997): doubling wealth while halving resource use — a 4×
improvement in resource productivity.
Factor 10 A more radical target proposed by Friedrich Schmidt-Bleek: wealthy nations cutting resource use by 90% (10×
more efficient), to leave ecological room for developing nations to grow.
Why Set Numerical Targets At All Vague commitments to "be more efficient" are unfalsifiable. A stated factor gives engineers and policymakers 
something concrete to design against.
PRINCIPLES OF SUSTAINABILITY 16

S E C T I O N 2 · A C R I T I C A L C A V E A T
The Jevons Paradox
Efficiency does not automatically reduce total consumption — sometimes it does the opposite.
In 1865, economist William Stanley Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines did not reduce Britain's coal consumption — they increased it, by making coal 
power cheaper and more widely used.
The Mechanism
Efficiency lowers the effective cost of using a resource 
— and lower cost usually increases demand, 
sometimes enough to outweigh the efficiency gain 
entirely.
A Modern Example
More fuel-efficient cars can lead people to drive more 
miles, or buy larger vehicles, partially or fully offsetting 
the fuel savings ("the rebound effect").
The Lesson For This Course
Resource efficiency (Factor 4, Factor 10, IPAT's "T" 
term) is necessary — but without a hard cap or price 
signal alongside it, efficiency gains can be consumed 
away.

Whether the benefits and burdens of development and environmental change are shared fairly.

S E C T I O N 3 · D E F I N I T I O N
What Is Social Equity in Sustainability?
Not simply "equality" — fairness that accounts for different starting points and different exposure to harm.
Distributive Justice Who actually receives the benefits of development — jobs, infrastructure, clean energy — and who bears its 
costs, like pollution or displacement?
Procedural Justice Who gets a genuine say in decisions that affect their environment and livelihood — and who is left out of the 
room entirely?
Why It Belongs Alongside Ecology and 
Economics
A technically efficient, profitable, low-emission project that devastates one community's livelihood is not 
sustainable — it has simply moved the cost onto people with the least power to resist it.

Environmental Justice: Where the Idea Comes From
Warren County, North Carolina (1982)
Protests against a PCB toxic waste landfill sited in a majority-Black, low-income county are 
widely credited as the birth of the environmental justice movement, later formalized in the 
influential 1987 "Toxic Wastes and Race" report.
Bhopal Gas Tragedy, India (1984)
A gas leak at a Union Carbide pesticide plant killed thousands immediately and affected 
several hundred thousand residents of a densely populated, low-income neighborhood —
still cited as one of the world's worst industrial disasters and a landmark environmental 
justice case.
The pattern in both cases: hazards are disproportionately sited near communities with the least political and economic power to resist them.

Economic Viability
Whether an activity can genuinely continue — once its full, true cost is actually counted.
26

S E C T I O N 4 · D E F I N I T I O N
What Is Economic Viability in Sustainability?
Not the same question as "is it profitable right now?"
The Working Definition Economic activity that can be sustained over the long term without depleting the natural and social capital it 
depends on to keep functioning.
Why Short-Term Profit Isn't Enough A business can be highly profitable while quietly depleting the soil, water, or community trust it needs to 
operate in ten years — profitable today, insolvent against reality tomorrow.
The Core Requirement: Internalizing 
Externalities
Prices must reflect the true cost of an activity — including environmental and social costs — or the market will 
systematically favor the least sustainable option.
PRINCIPLES OF SUSTAINABILITY 27

S E C T I O N 4 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
True Cost Accounting: Pricing an Externality
G I V E N
A product's market price: ₹100 per unit
Uncompensated pollution and health costs borne by the surrounding 
community: ₹30 per unit
This gap between market price and full cost is called an externality
F O R M U L A
True Cost = Market Price + Externalized Cost
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Add the externality to the market price: ₹100 + ₹30 = ₹130
2 The real cost to society is 30% higher than what the market price actually reflects
3 This is the same logic behind the Social Cost of Carbon (~$190/tonne, US EPA, 2023) covered in our carbon pricing lecture.
₹130 True Cost The community is effectively subsidizing the product by ₹30 per unit through unpriced pollution and health impacts — a hidden 
transfer the market price never shows.

Metrics That Go "Beyond GDP"
GDP counts all economic activity as positive — including activity that depletes the future. These frameworks try to correct for that.
Green GDP
Subtracts the estimated cost of 
environmental degradation and resource 
depletion from conventional GDP figures.
Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI)
Adjusts GDP for income distribution, 
environmental costs, and unpaid work 
like caregiving — capturing what GDP 
misses entirely.
Gross National Happiness 
(Bhutan)
Bhutan's own wellbeing-centered 
alternative to GDP, formally adopted as 
national policy, weighing culture, 
environment, and governance alongside 
economic output.
Human Development Index 
(HDI)
The UNDP's composite measure 
combining health, education, and income 
— used globally as a richer alternative to 
income alone.

B R I N G I N G I T T O G E T H E R
When the Four Principles Pull Against Each Other
In the real world, these four principles rarely align perfectly — genuine sustainability work is about navigating the tension between them.
Resource Efficiency vs. Social Equity Automation and efficiency gains can displace workers — efficiency for the planet can mean hardship for people, without 
a deliberate "just transition."
Economic Viability vs. Ecological Integrity Conservation often has real short-term costs, while ecological damage is frequently cheaper in the near term — until the 
true cost is counted.
Social Equity vs. Economic Viability Redistributive policies that improve equity can carry real short-term economic costs, testing political will.
Ecological Integrity vs. Resource Efficiency The Jevons Paradox again: efficiency gains can enable more total consumption, undermining ecological goals unless 
paired with hard limits.

L E C T U R E R E C A P
Four Principles, Recapped
1
Ecological Integrity
An ecosystem's composition, structure, and function — including its resilience to 
disturbance.
2
Planetary Boundaries
Six of nine boundaries already transgressed (Richardson et al., 2023) — the scientific 
evidence base for ecological limits.
3
Resource Efficiency
Achieving more value per unit of resource — the core goal is decoupling growth from 
environmental harm.
4
The IPAT Equation
Impact = Population × Affluence × Technology — a quantitative tool for reasoning about 
sustainability trade-offs.
5
The Jevons Paradox
Efficiency gains can increase total consumption rather than reduce it — a critical caveat, 
not a reason to abandon efficiency.
6
Social Equity
Fair distribution of both the benefits and burdens of development — distributive and 
procedural justice together.
7
Environmental Justice
From Warren County (1982) to Bhopal (1984): hazards are disproportionately sited near 
the least powerful communities.
8
Economic Viability
Activity that can genuinely continue — which requires internalizing externalities into 
true-cost pricing.
9
Beyond GDP
Green GDP, GPI, Bhutan's Gross National Happiness, and HDI all try to measure what 
GDP alone misses.
10 The Real Work
Genuine sustainability means navigating the honest tensions between all four principles 
— not pretending they never conflict.

S E T T I N G T H E S C E N E
What Are the Sustainable Development Goals?
A single global to-do list, agreed to by every UN member state.
The Agenda "Transforming our World: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development" — adopted by all 193 UN member 
states on 25 September 2015, entering into force 1 January 2016.
The Structure 17 Goals, 169 targets, and over 230 indicators — covering poverty, health, education, climate, and everything in 
between, all due by 2030.
The Predecessor The SDGs succeeded the Millennium Development Goals (2000–2015) — 8 goals that cut extreme poverty and 
child mortality sharply, but left environmental sustainability under-addressed.
The Promise The Agenda's defining phrase: to "leave no one behind" — every goal is meant to apply universally, to rich and 
poor countries alike.

B R I N G I N G I T T O G E T H E R
Climate Change Threads Through All 17 Goals
Not every goal is about climate — but every goal is affected by it, or affects it in return.
1–5 (People) Climate change is a threat multiplier — worsening poverty, hunger, disease, and inequality for the most vulnerable first.
6, 12, 14, 15 (Planet) The natural systems most directly damaged by, and most protective against, a warming climate.
13 (Planet) The direct goal — climate mitigation and adaptation as an explicit global target in its own right.
7–11 (Prosperity) The economic engine of the solution — clean energy, green jobs, and sustainable industry and cities.
16 (Peace) The institutional capacity that makes climate policy and disaster response actually enforceable.
17 (Partnership) The cooperative machinery — finance, treaties, and technology transfer — that makes global action possible at all.

The Agenda
193 countries, 17 goals, 169 targets, adopted 2015 — the world's shared to-do list 
through 2030.

People (1–5)

Planet (6, 12–15)
Water, consumption, climate action itself, oceans, and land — the environmental 
foundation.
4
SDG 13 Specifically
The direct climate goal, recognizing the UNFCCC as the primary negotiating forum.
5
Prosperity (7–11)
Clean energy, decent work, industry, equality, and cities — the economic engine of the 
solution.
6
Peace (16)
Strong institutions make climate policy enforceable; climate stress can itself drive 
conflict.
7
Partnership (17)
No single country solves this alone — every climate treaty in this course depends on 
SDG 17.
8
Direct vs. Indirect Links
Some goals (7, 13, 15) are directly about climate; others (4, 5, 16) are linked through 
compounding effects.
9
The Core Insight
Climate change is not one goal among seventeen — it is a thread running through all of 
them.
10 Your Role
Every goal has an engineering gap waiting to be filled — the question is only which one 
calls to you.
